On one hand, it lowers financing barriers for emerging cloud service providers to expand its customer base; on the other, it directly participates in profit distribution within the downstream computing market through revenue sharing, thereby extending its control further down the AI value chain.

NVIDIA noted that emerging AI companies have historically faced significant constraints in accessing capital-intensive infrastructure—even long-term contractual commitments have often been insufficient to secure financing for compute capacity procurement. This means that numerous AI-native firms, model developers, and inference service providers face lengthy delays when scaling their computing capabilities: site selection, power procurement, construction, and hardware commissioning—each step can take several months or even longer.
The promise of this new model is to realign economic structures so these groups can rapidly access full-stack accelerated computing capabilities without waiting for the traditional infrastructure build-out cycle to complete.

In other words, NVIDIA’s backstop commitment effectively serves as a credit enhancement tool, enabling emerging cloud service providers—who would otherwise struggle to obtain bank loans—to mobilize significantly larger amounts of capital and accelerate data center construction.
Strategic Intent: Breaking the Dominance of Large Customers
NVIDIA’s launch of these initiatives is grounded in a clear strategic context. Currently, a small number of large cloud service providers—including Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Oracle, Meta, and Google—purchase the majority of NVIDIA’s chip output. However, several of these companies are developing their own competitive AI chips, posing a potential threat to NVIDIA.
To reduce its reliance on these giant clients, NVIDIA has spent the past few years actively supporting a cohort of emerging GPU cloud service providers, such as CoreWeave. The newly announced 'AI Compute Partnership Program' represents a continuation and deepening of this strategy.
According to prior reporting by The Information, NVIDIA has also recently been negotiating to provide financial guarantees for OpenAI’s lease of a large data center in Ohio—an asset that, if fully built out at current prices for chips, labor, power, and other materials, could cost as much as $500 billion.

According to prior reporting by The Information, NVIDIA’s own researchers have also used GPU servers leased back from Lambda.

In September 2024, NVIDIA committed to purchasing all of CoreWeave’s unsold capacity through 2032 if CoreWeave failed to secure tenants, under a contract then valued at $6.3 billion. This move effectively alleviated investor concerns about CoreWeave’s highly leveraged business model and drove its stock price up nearly 30% within the following week.

NVIDIA's $82B quarterly revenue and Micron's 346% year-over-year sales surge confirm AI chips are driving an unprecedented memory demand cycle.
SK Hynix controls 58% of the HBM market, and its $26.5B Nasdaq debut finally gives U.S. investors direct access to NVIDIA's most critical chip supplier.

During a July 10 CNBC segment , Kristina Partsinevelos framed SK Hynix’s roughly $26.5 billion capital raise at $149 per American depositary share as a defining moment for the AI supply chain. The Korean memory giant controls approximately 58% of the high-bandwidth memory market, giving it a commanding position in the technology required to make NVIDIA’s most advanced chips work. The offering ranks as the second-largest share sale ever, trailing only SpaceX’s NASDAQ debut last month.
For U.S. investors, the debut closes a long-standing accessibility gap. SK Hynix has been the essential HBM supplier to NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ) throughout the AI buildout, yet trading in the Korean parent required navigating Seoul-listed shares. It also arrives as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s “largest infrastructure expansion in human history” creates extraordinary demand for a product that remains in short supply.
SK Hynix Controls the Memory Powering the AI Revolution

Micron and Samsung competitors split roughly 21% each … as per Counterpoint Research.” She added a blunter framing of the competitive stack: “SK Hynix is bigger, cheaper and closer to NVIDIA.”
Partsinevelos noted revenue is expected to triple to $235 billion this year, with the company committing over $720 billion in capital investment over the coming years, primarily in South Korea. A separate roughly $458 million from the U.S. CHIPS Act is earmarked for an Indiana advanced packaging facility.
New Supply Will Likely Not Arrive Until 2027
Memory prices have been incredibly strong due to tight supply. “None of that supply, though, arrives before late 2027, which keeps the memory shortage going and record-high prices intact for now,” Partsinevelos said. Passive flows may amplify the near-term move: “Berkeley estimates the stock could see up to roughly $14 billion in passive buying alone as it enters the major indices just over the next few months.”

CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said in the Q3 release that results “reflect the strategic value of memory in the AI era.”

What infrastructure planners should account for
The single most expensive part of Nvidia's next-generation AI rack is no longer just the GPU. According to a Morgan Stanley bill-of-materials analysis, memory now accounts for roughly a quarter of the total, and the overall system price has nearly doubled generation over generation. For any organization budgeting AI infrastructure for the second half of 2026 and beyond, that shift changes how the numbers should be built.
Morgan Stanley Research estimates that Nvidia 's Vera Rubin VR200 NVL72 rack will cost hyperscale cloud providers around $7.8 million per unit, up from roughly $4 million for the current GB300 NVL72 generation. The GPUs themselves are not the driver of the increase. The bank estimates Nvidia will charge about $55,000 per Rubin GPU and $5,000 per Vera CPU when sold in volume.
The memory line is where the cost concentrates. Morgan Stanley puts memory content per rack at about $2 million, a 435% jump from the prior generation, driven by a threefold increase in LPDDR5X capacity to 54 terabytes per rack plus roughly $1 million or more in 3D NAND storage that was virtually absent from earlier systems. First shipments are scheduled for the third quarter of 2026, with volume ramping in the fourth.
As a share of the bill of materials, memory rose from 5 to 10 percent on the GB200 to 25 to 30 percent on the VR200, while the GPU's share fell from roughly 63 percent to 51 percent.
Only a handful of companies buy racks at this scale. But the force behind the price, constrained supply of DRAM, NAND, and high-bandwidth memory against AI-driven demand, is the same one now raising component costs across the market. Contract DDR5 pricing has climbed sharply, and device makers including Samsung and Apple are expected to pass higher memory costs into upcoming products. The AI buildout and the price of the memory in a laptop are now tied to the same supply squeeze.
For enterprise technology buyers, that means memory has become a strategic budget variable rather than a rounding error, whether the purchase is a data center commitment or a fleet refresh.
Three considerations follow directly from the Morgan Stanley breakdown.
Model your AI spend on total system cost, not GPU count. The generation-over-generation story is that peripheral components, memory, printed circuit boards, networking, cooling, and power, are absorbing a larger share of every dollar. Budgets built around GPU headline prices will understate the real bill.
Treat memory supply as a scheduling risk, not only a cost. With memory representing a quarter or more of rack value and supply tight, availability and lead times deserve the same planning attention as accelerator allocation.
Revisit the build-versus-rent math. As rack prices climb toward $8 million and memory pricing stays volatile, the calculus between owning infrastructure and consuming cloud capacity shifts. Morgan Stanley notes that a hyperscaler self-sourcing certain memory modules could bring the rack price down to around $6.7 million, a reminder that procurement structure now materially moves the number.
Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform will deliver a step change in performance, and demand is not in question. What has changed is where the money goes. The AI infrastructure bill is increasingly a memory bill, and the organizations planning capacity for the next two years will be the ones that budget for the full system rather than the chip on the front of the box.

You are a senior hedge-fund analyst. A research topic was opened on the company from the item below. Write the one question the topic is judged on: what it asks, its answer ladder and its due day. The ladder is written once, from this item only, and is never rewritten. Write in English.

What the question asks
- A judged question concerns one figure for a named period or one event. Write a question, not an assertion. A figure or event must be able to determine the outcome on the due date. For a figure, the question names the period it covers or the day it is measured at, and the material that settles it. The question is read later by a judge who has only the question, the ladder and new evidence, never this item or the topic: it must stand on its own, naming the thing asked, any company relevant to that question, and any amount it includes in full, and never say "this item".
- A topic's wording may ask about more than one thing. Judge the one the topic's outcome names as what is tracked. List every other part of the topic's wording that the question leaves out, a second figure or event, a condition or a comparison, in not_judged, each with one sentence on why it is not the one tracked. Never fold two things into one ladder: "Will the regulator approve the drug for a second use, and how many patients will take it in the first year?" is judged on the approval when that is what its outcome names, and the patient count is listed; "How much will the carrier's fuel bill be next year, and will its pilots strike?" is judged on the fuel bill when that is what its outcome names, and the strike is listed.
- Return no_ladder with the reason, and ladder null, in six cases: the topic has no main figure or event, naming none, or naming several with none of them the main one; nothing in the topic can be checked on a date, which for an event means that neither the topic nor the item gives a date and the topic names no period, unless it is a pending regulatory decision, for which use the company's current fiscal year-end; the figure is a company's figure for a quarter or a half-year, which is evidence to a yearly question; the figure is for a year that has already ended on the item's day; the figure is for a year beyond next year, unless the topic's opens_as is binding_obligation; or the question belongs to another company or to a matter that no theme in the request's themes covers, in which case name that company or matter in the reason. Do not rewrite a figure for a year beyond next year as an event to keep it; a numeric completion target may define the state of an event that is itself the topic.

Whose question it is
- A question about the company's revenue, profit, share, product progress or its own obligations is about the company: object is its ticker, even when policy or macroeconomics drives it. A question about what happens in the world, such as licensing, interest rates or aggregate spending, rather than the resulting effect on one company, belongs to a theme: object is a theme id from the request's themes. A question about another company's own figure, or about a matter no listed theme covers, has no object here: return no_ladder.

The ladder
- Define concrete, verifiable conditions now. Do not write a ladder whose thresholds depend on an unspecified future target. Conditions must not overlap or leave gaps: exactly one must hold when resolved; avoid vague "partial" outcomes.
- A yes/no question about an event is answered in yes_no: the condition under which the answer is Yes (the event has happened by the due day) and the condition under which it is No. An event that can end in more than two states is answered in exactly five states, one state each: in company_states when the object is the company, in theme_states when it is a theme. Build them so that they cannot overlap or leave a gap: start from the outcomes that exclude one another (decided for, not yet decided, decided against), then divide one or two of them by a property that either holds or does not. A regulator reviewing a merger gives five such states, each read as the position on the due day: cleared with no conditions; cleared with conditions; blocked; not decided, a filing still pending; not decided, no filing pending (withdrawn, lapsed or closed). In company_states each state carries one of the labels Strongly bullish, Bullish, Neutral, Bearish, Strongly bearish, each used once, meaning good or bad for the business, with the Neutral state's condition saying what it is neutral against: the outcome the market expects when the item states one, otherwise the baseline you compare with; in theme_states each carries a short name of the state itself, each name different.
- A figure is answered in figure: its unit (USD, percent, count, GW, MW, TWD or multiple; other when it is none of these, the question then naming the unit), the one year it covers (written FY2027 for a company's figure, which uses its fiscal year; written 2026 for a theme's figure, which uses the calendar year) and exactly five ranges of that one figure. Each range has an inclusive lower bound lo and an exclusive upper bound hi. Money amounts are written in full (12000000000, not 12 billion); percentages use 73, not 0.73. The lowest range has lo null, the highest hi null; every other bound is a number.
- Fill exactly one of yes_no, company_states, theme_states and figure; the others are null.
- reference is what the market expects for this figure or event when the topic opens: a consensus, the company's guidance, the stated plan or deadline. Its words are copied from the item exactly, as one unbroken passage: not reworded, not reordered, and not taken from the topic. It carries its value when the item states it as a number; when the item gives the expectation in words alone, value is null: never supply a number the item does not state. The ranges of a figure state the outcome against a reference that has a value: the middle range holds that value, the outcome near what is expected, and the ranges on either side are outcomes above and below it. When the item states no expectation, reference is null; then, and when the reference has no value, the ranges are your own estimate of the outcomes that could happen.
- favourable_end, for a figure about a company: higher when a higher outcome is good for its business, lower when a lower one is, with one sentence why. A result and its direction are separate: capital spending can build capacity or hurt returns. For a theme's figure it is n/a.

The due day
- Set the due day when the question can be resolved. It falls after the item's day, and on or after the day the material that settles the question is published.
- For a figure, use its publication date, which falls after the end of the period the figure covers: stated when the topic or the item gives it, expected_publication when you set the day you expect it to be published. Company figures use the company's fiscal year: "this year" contains the item's publication day, and "next year" follows it; convert fiscal years using the fiscal-year note. Other figures use calendar years.
- For an event, name the date at which its outcome is assessed: stated when the topic or the item gives it; period_end when it is the last day of the period the topic names, or the company's current fiscal year-end for a pending regulatory decision that has no date.
- When the topic's opens_as is binding_obligation, the due day is at most 548 days (18 months) after the item: for an obligation already taken on, its next annual filing; for one not yet signed, the day by which the signing can be checked.

Memory Market Expert: “SK Hynix Is Bigger, Cheaper and Closer to NVIDIA.” Inside Its $26.5 Billion Nasdaq Debut
SK Hynix just pulled off one of the largest share sales in history, and one memory market expert says U.S. investors have been missing the single most critical bottleneck in the entire AI supply chain. Here is why that changes…
By Thomas Richmond
NVIDIA's $82B quarterly revenue and Micron's 346% year-over-year sales surge confirm AI chips are driving an unprecedented memory demand cycle.
SK Hynix controls 58% of the HBM market, and its $26.5B Nasdaq debut finally gives U.S. investors direct access to NVIDIA's most critical chip supplier.
Partsinevelos warned that no new HBM supply arrives before late 2027, keeping record prices intact while $14B in passive index buying looms.
CNBC's Kristina Partsinevelos reports on SK Hynix's significant $26.5 billion Nasdaq debut, highlighting its crucial role in the AI memory market alongside NVIDIA. © 24/7 Wall St.
During a July 10 CNBC segment , Kristina Partsinevelos framed SK Hynix’s roughly $26.5 billion capital raise at $149 per American depositary share as a defining moment for the AI supply chain. The Korean memory giant controls approximately 58% of the high-bandwidth memory market, giving it a commanding position in the technology required to make NVIDIA’s most advanced chips work. The offering ranks as the second-largest share sale ever, trailing only SpaceX’s NASDAQ debut last month.
For U.S. investors, the debut closes a long-standing accessibility gap. SK Hynix has been the essential HBM supplier to NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ) throughout the AI buildout, yet trading in the Korean parent required navigating Seoul-listed shares. It also arrives as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s “largest infrastructure expansion in human history” creates extraordinary demand for a product that remains in short supply.
SK Hynix Controls the Memory Powering the AI Revolution
The core setup for SK Hynix, according to Partsinevelos: “SK Hynix is the world leader in high bandwidth memory . The memory that feeds AI chips with roughly 58% of that market. Micron and Samsung competitors split roughly 21% each … as per Counterpoint Research.” She added a blunter framing of the competitive stack: “SK Hynix is bigger, cheaper and closer to NVIDIA.”
Partsinevelos noted revenue is expected to triple to $235 billion this year, with the company committing over $720 billion in capital investment over the coming years, primarily in South Korea. A separate roughly $458 million from the U.S. CHIPS Act is earmarked for an Indiana advanced packaging facility.
New Supply Will Likely Not Arrive Until 2027
Memory prices have been incredibly strong due to tight supply. “None of that supply, though, arrives before late 2027, which keeps the memory shortage going and record-high prices intact for now,” Partsinevelos said. Passive flows may amplify the near-term move: “Berkeley estimates the stock could see up to roughly $14 billion in passive buying alone as it enters the major indices just over the next few months.”
Readers looking for the broader thesis on companies riding this wave can dig into our Free Report: 7 Stocks Powering the AI Boom (That Aren’t Chipmakers) .
Micron Shows How Valuable AI Memory Has Become
SK Hynix’s U.S.-listed challenger, Micron Technology ( NASDAQ:MU ), shows why memory investors are watching HBM share so closely. Micron posted Q3 FY2026 revenue of $41.456 billion, up 345.7% year over year, with non-GAAP diluted EPS of $25.11 and GAAP gross margin of 84.6%. Guidance for the following quarter calls for revenue of $50.0 billion plus or minus $1.0 billion. CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said in the Q3 release that results “reflect the strategic value of memory in the AI era.”
Micron’s HBM4, built on 1-beta DRAM, is in high-volume shipments for its lead customer platform, and HBM4E is in development, with volume production expected in calendar 2027. Shares closed at $991.64 on July 9, up 247.66% year to date. Analysts maintain a consensus price target of $1,486, with the stock currently sporting a forward P/E of about 6.
NVIDIA’s Growth Is Creating an Unprecedented Demand Signal
On the demand side, NVIDIA reported Q1 FY2027 revenue of $81.62 billion, up 85.2% year over year, with Data Center revenue of $75.25 billion and total supply-related commitments of $119.0 billion. Shares closed at $202.78 on July 9. Every one of Nvidia’s Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems requires HBM stacks supplied at scale by SK Hynix today.
SK Hynix’s U.S. debut gives investors direct access to the company holding the strongest position in one of the AI buildout’s tightest bottlenecks. It controls roughly 58% of the HBM market, and new capacity will not materially alleviate the shortage before late 2027.
Partsinevelos closed with the industry’s most durable caveat: “The longer term risk, though, is that memory has never really met a supercycle that didn’t eventually crash .” History is unambiguous on that point. For now, the memory shortage is likely to persist into 2027, index inclusion should act as a mechanical bid for the stock, and the three players controlling roughly 95% of memory production remain in a pricing environment they have not enjoyed in over a decade.
